items.followUp: Name two other units used to express the concentration of a solution.

rubric.why: The student identifies one valid unit or method of expressing concentration.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for each valid unit named, up to 2 marks.

rubric.why: The question asks for any two units.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for a second valid unit; do not award twice for the same unit.

modelAnswer: Two units used to express concentration are molarity and molality.

items.followUp: Write any two characteristics of a suspension.

rubric.why: Colloids have several characteristic properties; any one valid property earns credit.
rubric.description: One correct characteristic of a colloids
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for any one correct property.

rubric.why: A second distinct property is required.
rubric.description: A second correct characteristic of a colloid
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for a second distinct property.

modelAnswer: Colloids are heterogeneous mixtures, although they may appear homogeneous to the naked eye.
Colloidal particles scatter light, producing the Tyndall effect.
Their particles do not settle on standing.

items.followUp: Define an alloy and give one example.

rubric.why: Alloying involves combining substances to form an alloy.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that alloying is the mixing or combining of metals, or of a metal with a non-metal.

rubric.why: A valid example demonstrates the meaning of alloying.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for any valid alloy, such as brass, bronze, steel or solder.

modelAnswer: Alloying is the process of mixing two or more metals, or a metal with a non-metal, usually in the molten state, to form an alloy.
For example, brass is made by mixing copper and zinc.

items.followUp: What are canal rays? State any three properties of canal rays.

rubric.why: Canal rays are streams of positively charged particles.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for identifying them as positively charged rays or streams of positive ions.

rubric.why: Their passage through holes in the cathode gives them their name.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that they pass through holes or canals in a perforated cathode.

rubric.why: Canal rays travel in straight paths.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for this property.

rubric.why: Their positive charge makes their deflection in electric or magnetic fields a characteristic property.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that they are deflected by an electric or magnetic field toward the negative plate.

rubric.why: Unlike electrons, canal-ray particles vary with the gas in the discharge tube.
rubric.description: Dependence on gas or variable properties
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that their nature or properties depend on the gas, or that their mass-to-charge ratio is not constant.

modelAnswer: Canal rays are streams of positively charged particles (positive ions) produced in a gas-discharge tube.
They pass through the holes or canals in a perforated cathode.
They travel in straight lines.
They are deflected by electric and magnetic fields toward the negative plate.
Their properties, including the mass and charge of their particles, depend on the gas present in the tube.

items.followUp: Describe any four other branches of Chemistry.

rubric.why: Physical Chemistry concerns the physical properties and behaviour of matter.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for a correct description of this branch.

rubric.why: Organic Chemistry studies carbon compounds.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for a correct description of this branch.

rubric.why: Inorganic Chemistry studies elements and their compounds, generally excluding most carbon compounds.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for a correct description of this branch.

rubric.why: Biochemistry studies the chemical processes and substances in living organisms.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for a correct description of this branch. Any four correctly described branches earn full marks.

modelAnswer: Physical Chemistry deals with the physical properties of matter and the laws and principles governing chemical changes.
Organic Chemistry deals with carbon compounds, especially hydrocarbons and their derivatives.
Inorganic Chemistry deals with elements and their compounds, generally excluding most carbon compounds.
Biochemistry deals with the chemical substances and processes occurring in living organisms.

items.followUp: Explain the formation of a coordinate covalent bond in the hydronium ion, H₃O⁺.

rubric.why: In a coordinate covalent bond, both shared electrons come from one atom.
rubric.description: Definition of a coordinate covalent bond
rubric.how: Award 2 marks for explaining that one atom donates both electrons of the shared pair to another atom.

rubric.why: The donating atom is the donor and the receiving atom is the acceptor.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for correctly explaining the donor/acceptor roles or identifying the lone pair donated by the donor.

rubric.why: Ammonia donates its nitrogen lone pair to H⁺ to form NH₄⁺.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for a correct explanation or representation of NH₃ donating a lone pair to H⁺ to form NH₄⁺.

rubric.why: Water can donate an oxygen lone pair to H⁺ to form H₃O⁺.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for a correct explanation or representation of H₂O donating a lone pair to H⁺ to form H₃O⁺.

modelAnswer: A coordinate covalent bond is a covalent bond in which both electrons of the shared pair are donated by one atom.
The atom donating the pair is the donor; the atom accepting it is the acceptor.
In NH₃ + H⁺ → NH₄⁺, nitrogen donates its lone pair to H⁺, forming a coordinate covalent bond.
In H₂O + H⁺ → H₃O⁺, oxygen donates one of its lone pairs to H⁺, forming a coordinate covalent bond.

items.followUp: Define evaporation and state three factors that increase its rate.

rubric.why: Evaporation is the escape of particles from the liquid surface into the vapour state.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for defining evaporation as the change of a liquid into vapour from its surface, below its boiling point.

rubric.why: Temperature, exposed surface area, air movement, humidity and the nature of the liquid affect evaporation.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for correctly stating how one factor affects the rate.

rubric.why: A second distinct factor is required.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for correctly stating how a second distinct factor affects the rate.

rubric.why: A third distinct factor is required.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for correctly stating how a third distinct factor affects the rate.

modelAnswer: Evaporation is the change of a liquid into vapour from its surface at a temperature below its boiling point.
Increasing the temperature increases the rate of evaporation because more molecules have enough energy to escape.
Increasing the exposed surface area increases the rate of evaporation.
Increasing wind speed or air movement increases evaporation, while increasing humidity decreases it.
Evaporation also depends on the nature of the liquid; more volatile liquids evaporate faster.

items.followUp: Compare alkali metals and alkaline earth metals in their reactions with water, oxygen and halogens.

rubric.why: Alkali metals generally react more vigorously with water than alkaline earth metals; their hydroxide and hydrogen products can also distinguish the reactions.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for a correct comparison of their reactions with water.

rubric.why: Alkali metals can form oxides, peroxides or superoxides, while alkaline earth metals generally form oxides.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for a correct comparison of the oxygen compounds formed.

rubric.why: Alkali metals form monovalent halides; alkaline earth metals form divalent halides.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for correctly comparing the halides formed, such as MX and MX₂.

rubric.why: Their different valencies lead to MH hydrides for alkali metals and MH₂ hydrides for alkaline earth metals.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for correctly comparing the hydrides formed.

modelAnswer: With water: Alkali metals react vigorously to form hydroxides and hydrogen; alkaline earth metals react less vigorously. Beryllium does not react with water, while magnesium reacts with hot water or steam.
With oxygen: Alkali metals may form oxides, peroxides or superoxides; alkaline earth metals generally form oxides.
With halogens: Alkali metals form halides of formula MX, while alkaline earth metals form halides of formula MX₂.
With hydrogen: Alkali metals form hydrides of formula MH, while alkaline earth metals form hydrides of formula MH₂.
